title: RBI's Draft Model Risk Management Guidance Would Bring AI and Spreadsheet Models Under Board Policy, Independent Validation, Human Oversight and a Kill-Switch Requirement
summary: The Reserve Bank of India's draft Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management, 2026, described in a June 24, 2026 consultancy analysis, would require a board-approved framework covering AI and machine-learning models, independent validation even of vendor models, explainability controls, disclosures and human switches for customer-facing AI, and human-oversight and kill-switch mechanisms.
description:
The Reserve Bank of India has released a draft framework for managing the risks of the models that regulated lenders use, with specific provisions for artificial intelligence and machine learning. The details in this article come from an analysis by the consultancy Vinod Kothari, dated June 24, 2026, of the RBI's draft Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management, 2026. The RBI's own press release and the draft text were not reviewed for this article. The analysis does not state the deadline for comments or an implementation date, so neither is given here. Some descriptions of the draft that circulated in press coverage list particular categories of lenders, and this article follows only what the analysis says.

Status and scope

The draft is out for public consultation, which means the RBI is inviting comments before finalising it. According to the analysis, it applies to all regulated entities, and the analysis specifically discusses non-bank financial companies in several categories. Once final, the guidance is intended to replace Chapter 3, on credit risk models, of the RBI's 2002 Guidance Note on Credit Risk Management. That is a notable detail: the old chapter dealt with traditional credit scoring and similar models, while the new text is written with AI and machine learning in mind.

What counts as a model

The definition is broad. A model is any system that takes inputs, applies processing logic and produces outputs that materially affect decisions. The analysis stresses that this applies whether or not the entity calls it a model, and that it includes spreadsheet-based tools. Its example is a loan pricing calculator that determines lending rates. A lender that thinks of a spreadsheet as just a spreadsheet may therefore find it in scope if it drives material decisions.

Governance requirements

The draft requires a model risk management framework approved by the board and covering AI and machine-learning models. Models are to be tiered by risk, and high-risk models need approval from the Risk Management Committee of the Board. Entities must keep a living model inventory, and decommissioned models must be retained for more than 10 years. The retention period is long, and it implies that entities must be able to reconstruct how an old decision was made.

Validation and vendors

Independent validation is mandatory. The analysis says the entity must validate a model independently even if a vendor provides its own certification. It also says entities need enhanced oversight from the board's risk committee regardless of risk tier, along with contractual rights to the vendor's technical documentation and to audit access. The analysis summarises the principle as: outsourcing a model does not outsource the risk. For lenders that buy scoring or fraud tools from technology firms, this is a significant obligation, since it means they must be able to examine what they buy.

Explainability and fairness

Credit underwriting models fall under material decision-making, which carries higher explainability thresholds. Where a model cannot be fully explained, the entity must add enhanced validation, output verification, more frequent monitoring and restrictions on use. On fairness, entities must identify the risk of discriminatory outputs, particularly in credit decisions, carry out fairness assessments and recalibrate or redesign models where necessary.

Customer-facing AI

For chatbots, voice bots and generative AI that interact with customers, the analysis lists several requirements. The customer must be told they are dealing with an AI or machine-learning system and what its limitations are. They must be able to switch to a human on request. The entity must apply system-level controls against hallucinations, which are fabricated outputs, and build protections against prompt injection, adversarial inputs and anomalous use. It must also run structured red-teaming and challenge testing, meaning deliberate attempts to make the system fail.

Human oversight and the kill switch

The draft requires human-in-the-loop or human-on-the-loop arrangements, kill-switch or override mechanisms and periodic human review of AI-driven decisions. A kill switch is a way to stop or override a model quickly when it behaves badly. The analysis notes that the draft specifically flags automation bias, the tendency of reviewers to accept a machine's answer, and decision fatigue among those reviewers. The requirement therefore goes beyond having a person nominally in the process: it asks whether the person can actually exercise judgment.

What is not in the analysis

Several things are not stated in the source: when comments are due, when the final guidance will take effect, whether any category of small entity will be exempt, and exactly how the tiers of risk are defined. Those will determine how much the draft changes day-to-day practice. Readers who must comply should consult the RBI's published draft.

What it means for insurers

The analysis concerns RBI-regulated lenders, and this article does not claim the draft applies to insurers, which are supervised by IRDAI. It is relevant to insurers only as a signal of how Indian regulators are approaching AI governance, and as a point of comparison for the AI work that IRDAI has begun.

Limits

This article relies on a consultancy's analysis of a draft, not on the RBI's own document. The draft may change after consultation. It is general information, not legal or compliance advice.
source_name: Vinod Kothari Consultants (analysis of RBI's draft guidance, June 24, 2026)
image_alt: Artificial intelligence concept representing model risk governance in finance (illustrative)
key_points: The draft Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management, 2026 is out for public consultation, applies to regulated entities including NBFCs and would eventually replace Chapter 3 (Credit Risk Models) of RBI's 2002 Guidance Note on Credit Risk Management.

A model is defined as any system that takes inputs, applies processing logic and produces outputs that materially affect decisions, whether or not the entity calls it a model, and the definition includes spreadsheet tools such as a loan pricing calculator.

Entities need a board-approved framework covering AI and machine-learning models, a risk-tiered approach with Risk Management Committee of the Board approval for high-risk models, and a living model inventory with decommissioned models kept for more than 10 years.

Independent validation by the entity is mandatory even when a vendor certifies a model, and customer-facing AI must disclose that it is AI, offer a switch to a human and be tested against hallucination, prompt injection and adversarial inputs.
The draft requires human-in-the-loop or on-the-loop oversight, kill-switch or override mechanisms and periodic human review, and flags automation bias and decision fatigue among reviewers.
why_it_matters: Lenders increasingly use automated models to decide who gets credit and at what price. The draft would treat those models as a source of risk that boards must own, which would reach beyond banks to non-bank lenders and any firm using vendor-built or AI-driven tools.

title: Al Wathba Insurance Becomes the First UAE Insurer to Access Lloyd's Through a London Bridge 2 Protected Cell, Backing a Portfolio of Over $100 Million of Premium
summary: In December 2025 Al Wathba Insurance invested in Cell 27 of Lloyd's London Bridge 2 protected cell company, becoming the first UAE-based insurer to access the Lloyd's market this way, with returns expected from an underlying portfolio of more than $100 million of global property and casualty premium from financial year 2026.
description:
Al Wathba Insurance has taken a route into Lloyd's of London that no insurer in the United Arab Emirates had used before. The transaction was reported in December 2025. Reinsurance News published the news on December 22, 2025 under the headline "Al Wathba Insurance secures access to Lloyd's of London", Artemis published its account on December 22 and updated it on December 23, and Business Insurance reported it the same day, citing Middle East Insurance Review, which had run the story on December 21 under the headline "AWNIC is first UAE insurer to access Lloyd's via London Bridge 2 protected cell structure."

The facts, as reported, are as follows. Al Wathba, which is based in Abu Dhabi and Dubai and trades on the Abu Dhabi exchange as AWNIC, completed its first capital allocation to Lloyd's through London Bridge 2, a vehicle sponsored by Lloyd's. It invested in Cell 27. Artemis reported that Vice Chairman H.E. Rashed Darwish Al Ketbi and chief financial officer Muralikrishnan R visited Lloyd's to complete the investment formally. Lockton Re structured the transaction and curated the portfolio of Lloyd's syndicates that receive the capital, with Gerard Monayer, Lockton Re's chief executive for the Middle East and North Africa, and James Mackay, head of Lloyd's capital, named in the coverage. The size of Al Wathba's investment was not disclosed. What was disclosed is that, starting in financial year 2026, the company expects to receive returns from an underlying portfolio of more than $100 million of global property and casualty premium.

Chief executive Shukri Almheiri said: "This milestone investment will provide Al Wathba Insurance with a significant competitive edge." He added that the company will use Lloyd's risk solutions and benefit from the investment returns the Lloyd's market has historically delivered. The company called the move a "pivotal moment in its growth journey" and described it as part of its strategy to diversify revenue and push into international business. Lockton Re's Mackay praised Al Wathba's speed and decision-making during the syndicate allocation process.

To understand what Al Wathba bought, it helps to look at the vehicle. A protected cell company is a single legal entity divided into separate cells, each of which holds its own assets and liabilities. Lloyd's own overview of London Bridge 2 describes it as the second multi-arrangement insurance special purpose vehicle that Lloyd's has sponsored, a "transformer" that turns insurance and reinsurance risk written at Lloyd's into equity or debt securities offered to institutional investors. It is an onshore company incorporated in England under the Risk Transformation Regulations 2017, authorised and supervised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and the Financial Conduct Authority. It is licensed to reinsure business underwritten at Lloyd's and to issue securities that fully fund its reinsurance obligations, and the overview describes it as tax transparent.

Each transaction runs through a segregated cell, which also issues the securities. Cell liabilities are ring-fenced for insolvency purposes, and each transaction is limited recourse, meaning the aggregate liability is capped at the cell's funded assets. Investors' rights are subordinated, under a priority of payments, to the party being reinsured. The company is owned by an orphan trust, with an independent board drawn from Lloyd's, Artex and Intertrust, and an underwriting committee approves transactions and the creation of cells, subject to quarterly board ratification. Users of the vehicle can be corporate members and Lloyd's syndicates, and capital providers are qualified investors such as institutional investors and private equity funds.

The overview describes two main structures. For members, the vehicle can provide reinsurance of a member's Funds at Lloyd's, using a whole-account quota share of up to 100% or an excess-of-loss cover, with capital assessed on a Solvency II basis. For syndicates, it can provide whole-account or variable quota share or excess-of-loss reinsurance, including catastrophe bonds, with no line-of-business restriction and a defined risk period typically aligned with existing annual reinsurance. The document says London Bridge 2 had issued over US$750 million of securities to institutional investors across 13 cells, including the first 144A catastrophe bond, though the document does not date that figure and it should be read as an earlier snapshot, since Cell 27 shows that the numbering has moved on. Case studies in the overview include US$171.5 million of preference shares issued through four cells in February 2023 for Ariel Re to support the 2023 underwriting of Syndicate 1910, and a US$100 million catastrophe bond for Beazley in December 2023. Neither of those involved Al Wathba. Lloyd's presents the vehicle as a more diversified source of capital for profitable growth as part of its "Future at Lloyd's" strategy.

For a UAE insurer, the attraction is access and diversification. Al Wathba earns premiums mainly from regional business, and an allocation to a portfolio of global property and casualty risks written by several Lloyd's syndicates gives it exposure that is not tied to the Gulf economy. The structure also means it does not have to set up a syndicate or hold a Lloyd's licence itself, and the limited-recourse design caps its downside to what it has put in. The reports do not say how much that is, and they do not describe fees, collateral arrangements, syndicate names or regulatory approvals on the UAE side, so those cannot be assessed.

What to watch next is whether other Gulf insurers follow, and how the portfolio performs once the financial year 2026 returns are reported. Property and casualty returns depend on catastrophe losses and on the pricing cycle, and rates in the Lloyd's market have been falling in 2026, as the market's own half-year results show. Al Wathba's own results disclosures are the place where investors should look for the actual return.
source_name: Reinsurance News (December 22, 2025), Artemis (December 22-23, 2025), Business Insurance (December 22, 2025) and Lloyd's London Bridge 2 Overview
image_alt: Gulf city skyline representing the UAE insurance market (illustrative)
key_points: Al Wathba Insurance, which operates from Abu Dhabi and Dubai, completed its first capital allocation to Lloyd's through Cell 27 of the London Bridge 2 protected cell company, reported on December 22, 2025 as a first for a UAE-based insurer.
Lockton Re structured the transaction and curated the portfolio of underlying Lloyd's syndicates; the amount invested was not disclosed.

Al Wathba expects returns from an underlying portfolio of more than $100 million of global property and casualty premium, starting in financial year 2026, and its chief executive Shukri Almheiri said the investment 'will provide Al Wathba Insurance with a significant competitive edge.'

London Bridge 2 is an English protected cell company incorporated under the Risk Transformation Regulations 2017 and supervised by the PRA and FCA; each transaction runs through a segregated cell whose liabilities are ring-fenced and limited in recourse to the cell's funded assets.

Lloyd's overview material says London Bridge 2 had issued over US$750 million of securities to institutional investors across 13 cells, including the first 144A catastrophe bond, and sets out structures for members' Funds at Lloyd's and for syndicate reinsurance.
why_it_matters: Most insurers that want exposure to Lloyd's must either run a syndicate or buy into one, both of which are heavy commitments. A protected cell lets an investor take a defined share of a portfolio of Lloyd's business through a ring-fenced structure, with risk and return limited to what is placed in the cell. For a regional insurer, that is a way to diversify beyond its home market. The transaction is small in public terms, since the amount was not disclosed, but it marks a first for the UAE and shows how Gulf insurers are using capital-market style structures.

title: G7 Central Banks' First Quantum Report Warns of 'Harvest Now, Decrypt Later' Risk and Calls for Preparation, While Stating It Gives No Operational Recommendations
summary: The G7 Central Bank Quantum Technologies Working Group, co-chaired by the Banque de France and the Bank of Canada, published its first report on June 11, 2026, setting out quantum risks to cryptography and possible uses in finance, with Governor Tiff Macklem saying the window to being quantum-ready is narrowing.
description:
On June 11, 2026, the Bank of Canada announced that a group of G7 central banks had published a report on quantum technologies and the financial system. The report, titled Preparing for Quantum Technologies: Key Considerations for Financial Sector Participants, is the first public deliverable of the G7 Central Bank Quantum Technologies Working Group. The report itself is dated May 2026 and is hosted by the Banque de France. This article uses the Bank of Canada's announcement and the report. The dates above are those shown by the sources.

Who is behind it

The working group was established in 2025. It is co-chaired by the Banque de France and the Bank of Canada, and its other members are the Deutsche Bundesbank, the Bank of England, the Banca d'Italia, the Bank of Japan, the Federal Reserve Board and the European Central Bank. Its stated purpose is to analyse the economic, financial and institutional implications of quantum technologies and to support dialogue among public authorities, financial institutions and technology stakeholders.

What kind of document it is

The report is deliberately modest in what it asks. The announcement describes it as institutional, analytical and non-prescriptive, with no operational recommendations, and the report itself says it does not anticipate regulation or prescribe actions. It gives a shared analytical framework and maps the landscape, including challenges, uncertainties and key questions. It builds on G7 central bank research, experiments and exchanges with academic and technology communities and says it will be updated as the group's work continues. It is therefore not a rule or a supervisory expectation. That distinction matters for firms wondering whether they have a new compliance obligation: on the evidence of these documents, they do not.

The security concern

The report's most concrete worry is about cryptography. Much of the encryption that protects digital communications, payments and financial data relies on mathematical problems that a sufficiently powerful quantum computer could solve. The report says no cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists yet. It cites expert assessments that put a non-negligible probability on one emerging within the coming decade, with estimates varying widely, and it gives no specific probability or date. The Bank of Canada's announcement likewise says the timing is uncertain while the potential impact is well understood.

The report highlights a threat known as harvest now, decrypt later. An attacker can copy encrypted data today and store it, planning to decrypt it once a capable quantum computer exists. Data that must stay confidential for decades is therefore at risk even though no quantum computer can break the encryption yet. The report adds that digital signatures could be affected over time, with possible consequences for tokenised assets, digital identity and distributed ledger systems.

Moving to new cryptography

The report notes that the U.S. standards body NIST has standardised several post-quantum cryptography schemes for key establishment and signatures. It stresses that migration is not a simple swap. It involves taking an inventory of cryptographic dependencies, testing compatibility, coordinating with counterparties and vendors, and building cryptographic agility, meaning the ability to change algorithms without rebuilding systems. There are trade-offs, including performance, larger keys and signatures, integration with older systems and interoperability during long transition periods. It also describes complementary approaches, including distributed symmetric key exchange and quantum key distribution, and says no single approach is universal.

The report points to a separate, earlier document: the G7 Cyber Expert Group published a quantum readiness roadmap in January 2026. According to a law-firm summary of that statement, it was published on January 13, 2026 by HM Treasury, is high-level and non-binding, sets out a phased approach covering awareness, inventory, risk assessment, migration and ongoing testing, and notes that many jurisdictions cite 2035 as the overall full-migration target, with the most important systems ideally upgraded around 2030 to 2032. The central bank report itself, as summarised here, does not set dates.

Opportunities in finance

The report is not only about threats. It says quantum computing may help with optimisation, simulation, sampling and risk analysis, and that it is best viewed as a specialised accelerator, similar to the way graphics processors are used. Possible uses include portfolio optimisation, pricing and risk modelling in markets, liquidity optimisation and anomaly detection in payments, and macroeconomic and financial stability modelling at central banks. The report is blunt about the present: applications are experimental, and classical methods still outperform quantum approaches in most practical settings. It adds that quantum-inspired methods can already run on conventional hardware.

Governance and system-level risks

The report raises several risks that go beyond cryptography. Reliance on a small number of providers, software stacks or hardware architectures could create correlated risks such as outages or supply-chain disruption. Advanced techniques may be hard to explain or validate, which challenges supervision and accountability. Adoption is likely to be uneven across institutions and countries, and skills are scarce. The Bank of Canada also notes that uneven preparedness across interconnected institutions could create system-wide vulnerabilities, which is why it says coordination matters.

The message from the Governor

Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem said that, with continuing advances in quantum computing, the window to being quantum-ready is narrowing. He said the report reflects collective efforts to improve understanding and promote preparedness. The announcement gives no deadlines.

What it means

For banks, insurers and market infrastructure, plausible first steps, drawn from the issues the report raises rather than from any instruction in it, are to know where cryptography is used, identify data with long confidentiality needs, ask vendors about their plans and follow the standards work. For ordinary customers, nothing changes today, and the report does not suggest that accounts are at immediate risk. Whether and when a quantum computer capable of breaking current encryption will be built remains uncertain, and this article does not predict it. Readers who need the detail should read the report and the Bank of Canada announcement. This article is general information and not security advice.
source_name: Bank of Canada (announcement of June 11, 2026) and the working group's report, hosted by the Banque de France
image_alt: Abstract technology visualization representing quantum computing (illustrative)
key_points: The Bank of Canada announced on June 11, 2026 that the G7 Central Bank Quantum Technologies Working Group, set up in 2025 and co-chaired by the Banque de France and the Bank of Canada, had published its first public deliverable; the report itself is dated May 2026.

The report is described as institutional, analytical and non-prescriptive, with no operational recommendations, and it calls for cooperation among central banks, public authorities and financial stakeholders.

Its main security concern is 'harvest now, decrypt later': data encrypted today could be decrypted by a future quantum computer, which matters most for information that must stay confidential for decades.

No cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists yet; the report cites a non-negligible probability that one could emerge within the coming decade, with estimates varying widely, and it avoids timeline predictions.

Quantum computing may help with optimisation, simulation and risk analysis in finance, but the report says applications are experimental and classical methods still outperform quantum approaches in most practical settings.
why_it_matters: Payments, bank communications and stored financial records all rely on encryption that quantum computers could eventually break. Central banks are signalling that firms should understand their exposure now, because switching cryptography across interconnected institutions takes years and uneven preparation could leave weak links in the system.
